passages.title: The clear proof and the religion commanded
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These five ayat explain why Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ at all. The world — both the People of the Book and the idolaters — is described as not departing from its condition until **al-Bayyinah**, "the Clear Proof," came to it: a Messenger reciting purified pages. And when that Proof arrived, the very people who had been waiting for it split over it. The passage ends (ayah 5) by stripping religion back to what was always commanded: sincere worship of Allah alone, prayer, and zakah.

The unity of the passage is a single argument: **a world awaiting the Proof → the Proof arrives → division follows → yet the command was never complicated.**

---

## The Prophet ﷺ recites this surah to Ubayy

Before the meaning, something about the honour of this surah. Ibn Kathir reports that **Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas bin Malik** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to Ubayy bin Kaʿb:

> "Verily, Allah has commanded me to recite to you: *Those who disbelieve from among the People of the Scripture…*"

Ubayy asked, "He (Allah) mentioned me by name to you?" The Prophet ﷺ replied, **"Yes."** So Ubayy wept.

Ibn Kathir notes that **Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i** all recorded this Hadith from Shuʿbah.

Sit with that for a moment. A man is told that the Lord of the worlds named him — a servant — and instructed His Messenger ﷺ to recite these words to him personally. Ubayy's tears are the right response to being addressed by Allah, and every reader of this surah is, in a smaller way, being addressed too.

---

## Ayah 1: a world in darkness, and the healer sent to it

**"The disbelievers from the People of the Book and the polytheists…"**

Ibn Kathir identifies the two groups plainly: the People of the Scripture are **the Jews and the Christians**; the idolaters are **the worshippers of idols and of fire, among the Arabs and the non-Arabs**. So the ayah gathers the whole religious landscape of the time — those with a revealed Book who had gone astray, and those with no Book at all.

The pivotal word is **munfakkīn** (منفكّين), rendered "were not going to leave" or "depart." Ibn Kathir reports **Mujahid's** explanation of it: *"they will not be finished until the truth becomes clear to them."* **Qatadah said the same thing.** That is the whole of the gloss the commentators give here, and it is enough: the turning point in their condition is the moment the truth becomes clear to them.

And what makes it clear is **al-Bayyinah** — the Clear Proof. Ibn Kathir says it means **this Qur'an**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the human scale of ayah 1. The entire world, it says, was sunk deep in the darkness of ignorance, superstition, corruption, disbelief and paganism. When the whole world was that benighted, the infinite grace, mercy and wisdom of the Lord of the worlds "bubbled up" to dispel the darkness, to cure the obnoxious diseases, and to dissipate the calamities that had become universal. The moral and spiritual maladies were acute, excruciating and severe — and such disease created the need for an effective, expert and competent healer. **That healer was raised in the person of the Final Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who is described here as al-Bayyinah, the Clear Proof.** And, as Maʿārif puts it, the healer came with a Book — which is why the ayat that follow list some of the Qur'an's important characteristics.

Notice what kind of ayah this is. It opens the surah not with a mere verdict on the world's condition but with the announcement of a remedy: darkness, then light sent into it; disease, then a healer raised for it.

---

## Ayat 2–3: what the Clear Proof actually is

Ibn Kathir observes the structure: Allah first says "the Bayyinah," then immediately **explains what the Bayyinah is** —

**"a messenger from Allah, reciting scrolls of ˹utmost˺ purity, containing upright commandments."**

Ibn Kathir: this means **Muhammad ﷺ and the Magnificent Qur'an he recites**, which is written down among the most high gathering in purified pages. He cites the parallel in Sūrat ʿAbasa: *"In Records held in honour. Exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes (angels). Honourable and obedient."* (80:13–16)

### The word *yatlū* — reciting

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the verb **yatlū**, from the infinitive **tilāwah**, "to read out or recite." But it makes a precise point: *not every reading or reciting is tilāwah — only the one that is very closely followed according to the teacher's instruction.* This, Maʿārif suggests, is probably why in common idiom **tilāwah** became the specific word for reciting the noble Qur'an. Recitation here is not casual reading aloud; it is faithful transmission of exactly what was received.

There is a discipline in that for us. The Qur'an is not a text one improvises with. It is received, then passed on as received.

### *Ṣuḥuf* and *kutub* — pages and writs

**Ṣuḥuf** is the plural of **ṣaḥīfah**: a leaf or page of a book, or sheets of paper on which something is written.

**Kutub** (plural of **kitāb**) could carry that same meaning — in which case *kutub* and *ṣuḥuf* would be synonyms. But Maʿārif argues the second sense of *kitāb* fits more appropriately here: a **writ**, as in "Had there not been a *writ* from Allah which came earlier…" (8:68). Why? Because the pronoun *-hā* in "**fīhā** kutub" refers back to the *ṣuḥuf*. If the two words were synonyms, the phrase *fīhā* would be rendered meaningless and the ayah would read "reciting purified written pages in which are true written pages" — and that, Maʿārif says, is **not in keeping with the lofty rules and principles of Qur'anic eloquence**.

So: the pages carry **divine writs**. This is a small grammatical observation with a large payoff: the Qur'an is not merely honoured speech on pure pages, it carries binding commands.

### *Muṭahharah* — purified

The adjective **muṭahharatan** describes the *ṣuḥuf*. Maʿārif reports from **Ibn ʿAbbās** that these Scriptures are **completely free from all possible flaws, forgeries, doubt, hypocrisy and deviations**.

Read that list against the state of the world in ayah 1 — corruption, superstition, distortion. The cure had to be uncontaminated to be a cure at all.

### *Qayyimah* — upright, or lasting

**Ibn Jarir** said of "wherein are upright Books": *"Meaning in the purified pages are Books from Allah that are upright, just and straight. They have no mistakes in them because they are from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic."*

Maʿārif adds a second possible sense. *Qayyimah* is used in the sense of "straight," describing *kutub* — that its laws, ordinances and injunctions are upright, straight, just and balanced. **But it could also mean "lasting and permanent"** — in which case the phrase signifies that the divine injunctions of the Qur'an **will last permanently till the Day of Judgment**. Both meanings are given; neither is presented as the only one.

### Why the mission itself was necessary

It is here — in its comment on verses 2–3, not on verse 1 — that Maʿārif states the point most directly. The verses, it says, purport to tell us that the sending of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ **as the Clear Proof was essential** to the transformation of the people of earlier revelations and the pagans, who had ended up in disbelief and **could not have departed from their erring ways without the help of his ﷺ Prophetic mission**. His mission was to recite to them the pure scrolls containing clear divine injunctions.

Maʿārif also makes a fine historical note here: initially the Prophet ﷺ did not recite from written Scriptures — **he recited from his memory** — but the sense of the ayah is that he recited to them a discourse that was later written and preserved in scrolls. And Maʿārif closes: the Qur'an, as the Clear Proof, is **the compendium of all that is good, lasting and immutable in teaching**.

---

## Ayah 4: they split *after* the Proof came

**"It was not until this clear proof came to the People of the Book…"** that they disagreed.

Maʿārif explains **tafarraqa** here as "to deny, reject, or differ and disagree."

This is the sharpest turn in the passage. One would expect clarity to *end* disputes. Instead, the arrival of clarity is precisely when the splitting began. Ibn Kathir links it to Āl ʿImrān: *"And be not as those who divided and differed among themselves after the Bayyināt came to them. It is they for whom there is an awful torment."* (3:105) He explains that this refers to the peoples of the revealed Scriptures sent down to the nations before us: after Allah established the proofs and evidences against them, **they divided and differed concerning what Allah had intended in their own Scriptures**, and their differences were many.

Ibn Kathir then cites — as something "reported in a Hadith that has many routes of transmission" — the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ that the Jews differed until they became seventy-one sects, the Christians seventy-two, and that this Ummah would divide into seventy-three, all of them in the Fire except one. When they asked, "Who are they, O Messenger of Allah?" he ﷺ replied: **"(Those who are upon) what I and my Companions are upon."** *(Ibn Kathir does not name a collection for this narration, so it is conveyed here exactly as he conveys it.)*

### Why this rejection was so strange

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān dwells on the tragedy of it. The People of the Book had **eagerly awaited** the advent of a great Prophet ﷺ about whom clear prophecies stood in their own Scriptures — including that the Qur'an would descend upon him and that it would be compulsory for them to obey and follow him. Yet when he actually appeared, instead of accepting him, they rejected him.

The Qur'an points to their prior agreement on this: *"…while earlier, they used to seek help against those who disbelieved…"* (2:89). Maʿārif explains that the Torah had foretold his coming in several places, and that the Jews themselves used to tell the pagan Arabs that a new Prophet was soon to come who would vanquish them — and that they would be with him and so be victorious. Then the same ayah continues: *"…yet when there came to them that which they did identify, they denied it."* Maʿārif notes that "that which they did identify" may refer to the Final Messenger ﷺ, or to the new Divine Book, or to the religion of Truth.

Maʿārif calls it "a strange phenomenon": before his advent they believed in him **without a single dissenting voice**; when he appeared as the Clear Proof, dissension arose — many accepted the new Prophet ﷺ, the new Book and the new religion on the strength of the prophecies in their own Scriptures, but a large number, especially the Christians, rejected them, while a small number believed.

**One precise observation from Maʿārif:** ayah 1 includes the pagans, but ayah 4 speaks only of "those who were given the Book," because this particular phenomenon was restricted to the People of the Book. Maʿārif closes that point with *"Allah knows best!"*

The lesson is uncomfortable and universal: **knowing the truth in advance is no protection against rejecting it when it arrives and costs something.**

---

## Ayah 5: the command was never complicated

**"even though they were only commanded to worship Allah ˹alone˺…"**

After all that division, Allah restates the entire demand in one ayah. Ibn Kathir highlights the exclusivity: *"And they were commanded not, but that they should worship Allah, making religion purely for Him alone."* He connects it to al-Anbiyāʾ: *"And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: there is no deity except Me, so worship Me."* (21:25)

**Mukhliṣīna lahu-d-dīn** — making the religion purely His. This is *ikhlāṣ*: the act belongs to Allah alone, undivided, unshared with any audience or motive.

**Ḥunafāʾ** — Ibn Kathir defines it as **avoiding shirk and being truly devout to tawhīd**. He cites an-Naḥl: *"And verily, We have sent among every Ummah a Messenger (proclaiming): 'Worship Allah, and avoid the Ṭāghūt (false deities).'"* (16:36) *Ḥanīf*, then, is not merely believing in One Allah; it is a **turning away** from everything false in the same motion as turning toward Him. (Ibn Kathir notes that the word *ḥanīf* has already been discussed previously and in Sūrat al-Anʿām, so he does not repeat it.)

Then two concrete obligations:

- **"and that they perform Salah"** — Ibn Kathir: *this is the best of the physical forms of worship.*
- **"and give Zakah"** — Ibn Kathir: *this is doing good to the poor and the needy.*

The order is exact. Sincerity of the heart, then the body's finest act, then the wealth's obligation to the vulnerable. Religion as Allah defines it reaches inward, upward, and outward.

### "And that is the right religion"

**Dhālika dīnu-l-qayyimah.** Ibn Kathir gives two senses: **the upright and just religion**, or **the nation that is straight and balanced.**

Maʿārif notes a grammatical difference among the scholars: **qayyimah** is apparently the qualifier of the noun **kutub** (the Books mentioned earlier), while **some treat it as qualifying the noun *millah*** (religion). Both are reported.

Maʿārif's summary of the ayah's purpose is worth carrying away: Allah commanded the People of the former Scriptures to render full and sincere obedience to the divine commandments — to worship Allah alone, establish the regular prayers, and pay the obligatory alms. Then the Qur'an reminds them that **this is not their distinctive feature exclusively**. All former religions that are upright and received Books from Allah have the same features. This is the true religion of all the Prophets (ʿalayhim as-salām), which they preached to their respective peoples. And taking *kutubun qayyimah* as referring, contextually, to the Qur'anic ordinances and injunctions, the ayah then means: **the ordinances of the Sharīʿah of Muhammad ﷺ are exactly the same as those that were given to them in their revealed Scriptures — not divergent — so they had no pretext to oppose.**

---

## Living it

Read as a whole, the passage does three things to the reader.

**First, it locates you.** Ayah 1 describes a world sunk in darkness and awaiting the Clear Proof, and Maʿārif — commenting on ayat 2–3 — says plainly that the Prophet's ﷺ mission was essential, because those people could not have departed from their erring ways without it. Guidance is a gift that arrived, not an achievement.

**Second, it warns you.** Ayah 4 shows that division is a real hazard *for people who have the truth*, not only for those without it. The Prophet's ﷺ answer about the one surviving group — those upon what he and his Companions were upon — is the measure given in the sources themselves.

**Third, it simplifies you.** Ayah 5 will not let religion become a tangle of identity and argument. Strip it back: worship Allah, purely for Him, turning away from all false objects of worship; establish the prayer; give the zakah. **That is the straight religion** — and, as Maʿārif points out, it is the same religion every upright Book-receiving community was given before.

Ubayy bin Kaʿb wept when he learned Allah had named him for these words. The words themselves are simpler than we make them.

passages.title: Worst of creation and best of creation
passages.tafsir:
## The two verdicts

These three ayat close the sūrah with a verdict. Humanity is sorted into two groups and given two names: **the worst of creation** and **the best of creation**. Ayah 6 names the first and states their end; ayah 7 names the second; ayah 8 unfolds what the second group receives, rising step by step until it reaches something Ibn Kathir says outweighs Paradise itself.

Ibn Kathir titles his comment on these three ayat exactly this way: *"Mentioning the Worse and Best of Creation and Their Recompense."* That is the unit. Read the three together and you feel the balance — a short, closed sentence for the losing side, and a long, opening, widening sentence for the winning side.

## "The worst of creation" — ayah 6

Ayah 6 speaks of *"those who disbelieve from the People of the Book and the idolaters."* Ibn Kathir explains that these are the wicked disbelievers who **oppose the Books Allah revealed and the Prophets whom He sent**. That is the defining feature Ibn Kathir points to: not merely ignorance, but opposition to revelation and to the messengers who brought it.

Their end is stated with no softening: they *"will abide in the fire of Hell."* Ibn Kathir presses on each word of the permanence: this means **"they will remain in it and they will have no way out of it and they will not cease being in it."** Three phrases for one reality — no exit, no interruption, no end.

Then comes the title: **ulāʾika hum sharr al-bariyyah** — *"they are the worst of creation."* Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase as: *"they are the worst creation that Allah has fashioned and created."* Notice the measure he uses. The comparison is not narrowed down; it is against what Allah has fashioned and created.

## "The best of creation" — ayah 7

Ayah 7 answers with the same grammar and the opposite verdict: *"Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds — they are the best of creation."*

Note how Ibn Kathir reads the two halves of the description. He says Allah here informs about the righteous **"who believed in their hearts and performed righteous deeds with their bodies."** Faith is located in the heart; righteous action is located in the limbs. The inward conviction and the outward life are named together, and Ibn Kathir keeps them paired.

**A remarkable point.** Ibn Kathir records that **Abu Hurayrah and a group of the scholars used this ayah as proof that the believers have a status among the creatures that is better than the angels** — precisely because Allah says *"they are the best of creation."* Ibn Kathir reports it as their view, and it is worth sitting with what it implies about you. The believer, by Allah's own naming here, is not a lesser being consoled with a garden.

Notice also what the ayah asks for. Two conditions only: belief, and righteous deeds.

## The reward, layer by layer — ayah 8

Ayah 8 does not simply say "they get Paradise." It builds.

**"Their reward with their Lord"** — Ibn Kathir: *"meaning, on the Day of Judgement."*

**"Gardens of ʿAdn, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever."** On this permanence Ibn Kathir gives one of his most beautiful glosses: **"having no end, no break and no conclusion."** Every earthly pleasure has all three — it finishes, it is interrupted, it concludes. This one has none of them. And notice that the same permanence that sealed the Fire in ayah 6 now seals the Garden in ayah 8. The two destinies are equally final.

**"Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him."** Here the ayah steps up onto a higher level altogether. Ibn Kathir says plainly: **"The condition of Him being pleased with them is more illustrious than all of the everlasting delights that they will be given."** All of it — the gardens, the rivers, the endless abiding — is outweighed by the single fact that Allah is pleased with them.

And the second half, *"and they are pleased with Him"* — Ibn Kathir: **"Due to the comprehensive favours He has given them."** The pleasure runs both ways. He is pleased with them; they are well-pleased with Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this verse points to *"the highest stage of spiritual development of the inmates of Paradise, that is, the Divine pleasure with no danger of Divine displeasure."* That last clause is the heart of it. This, Maʿārif adds, *"is the greatest reward with which the people of faith will be blessed."*

## From the Sunnah

**The conversation in Paradise.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a narration of Sayyidnā Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him), which it attributes to al-Bukhārī (through Mazhari). The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Allah shall address the inmates of Paradise: *"O Inmates of Paradise!"* They will reply that they are present and ready to carry out His orders, and that all good is in His control. He will ask them: **"Are you happy?"** They will submit, *"How can we not be happy when You have given us what You have not bestowed on any of Your creation?"* Allah will tell them: **"Shall I not grant you something superior to all of this?"** They will exclaim, *"What can be superior to this?"* And He will reply: **"I shall grant you My pleasure, and I will never be angry with you in the future."**

That narration is simply ayah 8 turned into a scene. The people of Paradise themselves cannot imagine anything beyond what they already have — and Allah tells them there is something beyond it, and it is His riḍā.

**Who the best and worst of creation actually are.** Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked: *"Shall I not inform you of the best of creation?"* They said, *"Of course, O Messenger of Allah!"* He said: **"A man who takes the reins of his horse in the way of Allah, and whenever there is a fearful cry from the enemy, he climbs upon it."** Then again: *"Shall I not inform you of the best of creation?"* They said, *"Of course, O Messenger of Allah!"* He said: **"A man who has a flock of sheep and he establishes the prayer and gives the obligatory charity."** Then: *"Shall I not inform you of the worst of creation?"* They said, *"Of course."* He said: **"The person who is asked by Allah and he does not give by Him."**

Look at the two "best" examples side by side. One is a man ready for danger, mounted at the first alarm. The other is a man with his flock of sheep, who simply keeps up his prayer and gives the obligatory charity. The Prophet ﷺ gave them the same title. The quiet life of a shepherd is not a lesser tier; his steadiness is named alongside the readiness of the other man.

And the "worst": a person who is asked **by Allah** — in Allah's name — and does not give. Set against the disbelievers of ayah 6, who Ibn Kathir says oppose Allah's revealed Books and His Prophets, the thread running through both is a heart to which Allah's claim carries no weight.

## The closing condition: "for him who fears his Lord"

The passage ends: *dhālika liman khashiya rabbah* — **"That is for him who fears his Lord."** One short clause holding the key to everything before it.

Ibn Kathir explains it as the reward *"that will be attained by those who revere Allah and fear Him as He deserves to be feared"* — and then defines that person precisely: **"This is the person who worships Allah as if he sees Him, and he knows that even though he does not see Him, indeed Allah sees him."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes its closing comment to clearing up what this "fear" actually is, and the correction matters. The word 'fear' or 'awe' here, Maʿārif insists, *"is not used in the sense of an 'agitated, disturbed or perturbed feeling' which we naturally have for an enemy, a beast, a ferocious animal or an obnoxious thing that might harm us."* But **khashyatullāh** — Allah's awe — is, on the contrary, *"a feeling of deep, reverential awe that leads man to Allah's obedience."* It is the awe of Allah's Majesty and His Incomparability that makes *"the perfect slave do every work under every circumstance to attain the Divine pleasure and evade every occasion of His displeasure."*

Maʿārif then makes a striking claim about this single quality: **"This is the axis on which rotates the religious perfection and all bounties of the Hereafter."** Not one virtue among many — the axle the whole wheel turns on.

## Two kinds of being pleased

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a distinction worth carrying away. There are **two types of riḍāʾ (pleasure)** — one in the general sense, and one in the specific or higher sense:

**The general sense** — *riḍāʾ bi'l-qadr*, to be pleased with every decree of Allah. Maʿārif says this is part of the obligations of a servant of Allah, and describes the consummated servant as one who *"is only ever satisfied and content with Allah Himself, and thus sincerely accepts the Divine decree."* Content with Allah — not merely with what Allah gives.

**The higher sense** — which is how Maʿārif says the word is used here: that **Allah bestows upon a servant all his specific wishes and ambitions without leaving out any of them**. Maʿārif links this to Allah's word to His Prophet ﷺ in 93:5, *"And of course, your Lord will give you so much that you will be pleased."*

And Maʿārif records — citing Mazhari — that when that verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ expressed his wish and ambition: **that he would not be pleased until every single believer is taken out of Hell.** That is what the Prophet ﷺ wanted for himself out of an open promise of satisfaction. His riḍāʾ was tied to ours.

## Living it

- **The two titles are earned, not assigned.** Ayah 7 names belief and righteous deeds. Ibn Kathir keeps them paired — belief in the heart, righteous deeds performed with the body. Ask honestly which of the two you have been neglecting.
- **The quiet life counts.** The man with his flock, establishing the prayer and giving the obligatory charity, was named among the best of creation alongside the man mounted for battle.
- **Be careful whom you refuse.** The worst of creation, in that narration, is the one who is asked by Allah — in His name — and does not give.
- **Aim past the Garden.** Ibn Kathir says Allah's pleasure is more illustrious than all the everlasting delights; the narration in Maʿārif shows the people of Paradise learning this from Allah Himself. Let your duʿāʾ ask for His riḍā, not only for His Garden.
- **Rebuild your idea of "fear."** If fear of Allah makes you flee Him, Maʿārif says you have the wrong feeling. Khashyatullāh *leads* a person to Allah's obedience. Its practical form is Ibn Kathir's description: **worship Allah as if you see Him — and know that though you do not see Him, He most certainly sees you.**

Two names, two ends, and one condition holding the whole thing together. The sūrah closes not on the gardens or the rivers but on a person: the one who reveres his Lord and fears Him as He deserves to be feared, who lives as though he sees Him — and who is brought, in the end, to the day his Lord tells him He is pleased with him and will never be angry with him again.
